newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Contours taking shape for future EU treaty.
newsitem.headline: Contours taking shape for future EU treaty.

text.p: Despite contrasting visions among its members of how the European Union should evolve, the contours of treaty reforms which EU leaders have promised to complete by mid-1997 are starting to become clearer.
At a summit on Saturday, EU leaders pledged to press on with negotiations to prepare their bloc for an influx of new members from eastern Europe and the Mediterranean early next century.

But behind the concern about the potential for failure in the inter-govermental conference (IGC), due to end in Amsterdam in June next year, negotiators and officials say a slow coming-together has already taken place on the main issues.

These include foreign policy, justice and home affairs, employment, institutional reform and -- perhaps most significantly -- developing the concept of flexibility which allows groups of countries to integrate at their own pace.
French President Jacques Chirac, speaking to reporters after the summit, said there was now wide commitment to strengthening the Common Foreign and Security Policy procedures.

This is likely to be done through creation of a forward planning unit to collate and coordinate the views of member states on foreign policy issues. The idea is that when a crisis blows up, the EU will already know where it stands.
The question of who will head the unit -- a senior bureaucrat or a high-profile public figure -- remains at issue.
On Third Pillar justice and home affairs, there is widespread agreement that the current system, where decisions are taken inter-governmentally, is not doing enough.
The leaders, however, are keen to change this, seeing the EU actions on crime and immigration as a playing a direct role in making the bloc more meaningful to its citizens.
"We spent a lot of time (at the summit) talking about crime and the fight against drugs," Chirac said.

Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, current chairman of the IGC, told the summit the new treaty would keep the inter-governmental nature of the Third Pillar, but that some Community decision-making procedures would have to be adopted.
In another attempt to make the EU popular, many leaders have also been insisting on an "Employment Chapter" in the treaty, formalising job creation as a goal of the bloc.

Although Britain, France and Germany -- three big players -- are hesitant or downright opposed to the idea of getting the EU involved in a national responsibility like employment policy, it is widely accepted that there will be some language included.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl signalled some flexibility on the subject at the summit, saying he could not rule out an "impulse" in that direction.
It is expected that the treaty could set up an Employment Committee to study jobs policy in much the same way that the Monetary Committee monitors monetary issues.
The biggest difficulty facing negotiators is changing the way EU institutions work in order to make them efficient in an enlarged bloc, reforms which would threaten the present balance of power.

Countries are naturally hestitant to give up the right to veto proposals they do not like or to lose the right to appoint an EU commissioner or serve as EU president -- even if such moves are seen as essential for the bloc to work.

A recent Irish attempt to get countries to specify the policy areas where they would be willing to give up their veto produced only a few concrete replies, although Britain quickly restated its outright opposition to any more Qualified Majority Voting.

In an address to his colleagues, however, Chirac pointed to one way around the impasse, noting that there was a link between abandoning unanimity and changing the voting system to give even more weight to bigger countries in the Council of Ministers.
Another way to overcome the different agendas and to allow a body built for six founder members to work with two dozen, is to make the organisation more flexible.
Officials say the new treaty is almost certain to grant countries that want to integrate faster than others the right to do so without necesarily being held up by the reluctant.

Such a concept is already in effect regarding the single currency, the Schengen agreement on borders, and Britain's opt-out of the Social Chapter, but some worry that such a trend may end up dividing rather than uniting Europe.
